title: Indian Contract Act, 1872 — Section 7 (Acceptance must be absolute)

content.overview: Section 7 provides that in order to convert a proposal into a promise, the acceptance must be absolute and unqualified, and be expressed in some usual and reasonable manner, unless the proposal prescribes the manner in which it is to be accepted. If the proposal prescribes a manner of acceptance and the acceptance is not made in that manner, the proposer may, within a reasonable time after the acceptance is communicated to him, insist that his proposal shall be accepted in the prescribed manner, and not otherwise; but if he fails to do so, he accepts the acceptance.
content.glance: Acceptance must be absolute and unqualified; usual/reasonable manner unless prescribed; non-prescribed manner may still bind if proposer does not insist.
content.study: To convert a proposal into a promise, acceptance must be absolute and unqualified, and expressed in a usual and reasonable manner unless the proposal prescribes a manner. If a prescribed manner is not followed, the proposer may within a reasonable time insist on the prescribed manner; failure to insist amounts to accepting the acceptance. Conditional acceptance is a counter-offer, not acceptance. Current-law framing: test absolute and unqualified assent; test manner; apply the prescribed-manner rule if relevant.

sections.heading: Absolute and unqualified
sections.body: Acceptance must be absolute and unqualified to convert a proposal into a promise.

sections.heading: Manner of acceptance
sections.body: Usual and reasonable manner unless the proposal prescribes a manner.

sections.heading: Prescribed manner not followed
sections.body: Proposer may within a reasonable time insist on the prescribed manner; failure to insist accepts the acceptance.

examples.title: Conditional reply
examples.body: A offers to sell for ₹5 lakh. B replies agreeing only if tyres are replaced. That is not absolute acceptance; it is a counter-offer.

hypotheticals.question: Is a conditional acceptance a valid acceptance?
hypotheticals.analysis: No. Section 7 requires acceptance to be absolute and unqualified; a condition is a counter-offer.

misconceptions.trap: Any reply that shows interest is acceptance.
misconceptions.correction: Acceptance must be absolute and unqualified under s. 7.

questionsAndAnswers.question: How should a Section 7 problem be analysed?
questionsAndAnswers.answer: I. Test absolute and unqualified assent. II. Test manner (usual/reasonable or prescribed). III. Apply prescribed-manner insistence rule if relevant. IV. Conclude.

examTips: Absolute and unqualified is the core test.
